headline: Paying students to sleep improves rest and grades

sources.title: Sleep payments: could they lead to better rest and better health? (The Guardian)
We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours and their grades quickly improved (The Conversation)
Incentives to sleep boost college students' grades, new study finds (University of Pittsburgh, via EurekAlert!)

chunks.text: A new study shows that paying college students to sleep can improve their sleep and their grades. [[Economists]] at the University of Pittsburgh {{handed out}} [[wearable sleep trackers]] to more than 1,100 [[undergraduates]]. The trackers [[recorded]] how long each student slept. For four weeks, 468 of the students earned about $5 for each night they slept at least seven hours. The study {{came out}} in July in the Journal of Political Economy. It drew [[widespread attention]] in September.

verbs.correct: To give something to every member of a group
verbs.wrong: To give control of something to another person
verbs.why: Teachers hand out tests at the start of class, and volunteers hand out water at a race. The economists handed out wearable sleep trackers to more than 1,100 students.

verbs.correct: To be published or made public
verbs.why: A new report comes out every spring, and her first novel came out last year. The study came out in July in the Journal of Political Economy.

chunks.text: At the start, the students slept 6.6 hours a night on average. Half of them usually {{stayed up}} past 1 a.m. They {{fell short of}} seven hours on more than half of [[school nights]]. Many students did not know how little they slept. Two-thirds said they usually got seven hours. The trackers showed that only about a third of the students reached that [[target]] on at least three nights out of five.

verbs.correct: To not go to bed until late
verbs.wrong: To remain at home for the evening
verbs.why: Kids like to stay up on New Year's Eve, and many students stay up before a big exam. Before the study, half of the students usually stayed up past 1 a.m.

verbs.correct: To fail to reach a goal or amount
verbs.wrong: To use something when other plans fail
verbs.why: A charity can fall short of its fundraising goal, and a runner can fall short of her target time. The students fell short of seven hours of sleep on more than half of school nights.

chunks.text: The paid students reached seven hours on 26 percent more nights than students who were not paid. They slept about 19 more minutes per school night. They also {{cut back on}} [[screen use]] late at night. The extra sleep {{paid off}} [[modestly]] in class. Their [[grade point average]], on a scale where an A equals 4, {{went up}} by about 0.08 points that [[semester]]. [[First-year students]] {{stood out}}, with the biggest [[gains]].

verbs.correct: To use or do less of something
verbs.wrong: To interrupt someone who is speaking
verbs.why: Many people cut back on sugar to lose weight, and families cut back on gas when prices rise. The paid students also cut back on screen use late at night.

verbs.correct: To bring a good result after effort
verbs.wrong: To make two people compete with each other
verbs.why: Hours of practice paid off when she won the race, and careful saving pays off when you buy a home. The extra sleep paid off modestly in class, with slightly higher grades.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher level
verbs.why: Rent often goes up every year, and the price of coffee went up last month. The paid students' grade point average went up by about 0.08 points that semester.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.wrong: To support someone in a hard time
verbs.why: A tall player stands out in a crowd, and a bright yellow car stands out in a parking lot. First-year students stood out in the study, with the biggest gains in sleep and grades.

chunks.text: After the payments ended, the students {{kept up}} part of the new [[habit]]. They still slept about eight minutes more per night for the next three to four weeks. Their grades stayed higher the next semester, but the effect {{wore off}} after that. [[Bedtime reminders]] without money had little effect. The hard part was {{following through}} [[night after night]]. The researchers say late-evening [[deadlines]] to {{turn in}} work can make it harder for students to sleep enough.

verbs.wrong: To hide some facts from others
verbs.why: It is hard to keep up a new exercise routine, and some people keep up a diet for only a week. After the payments ended, the students kept up part of the new habit, sleeping about eight extra minutes a night.

verbs.correct: To slowly become weaker and disappear
verbs.wrong: To make someone feel very tired
verbs.why: The effect of coffee wears off after a few hours, and the numb feeling from a dentist visit wears off by evening. The grade boost lasted into the next semester, but then it wore off.

verbs.correct: To finish what you planned to do
verbs.wrong: To ask again about something later
verbs.why: Many people make big plans in January but never follow through, and a good coach helps players follow through on their goals. Nearly all the students wanted more sleep, but the hard part was following through night after night.

verbs.correct: To give finished work to be checked
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or request
verbs.why: Students turn in essays at the end of the week, and workers turn in reports for their boss to review. The researchers say late-evening deadlines to turn in work can make it harder for students to sleep enough.

mainIdea.s: A study paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least seven hours. They slept more, their grades rose a little, and some benefit lasted after the money stopped.
mainIdea.why: Paid students reached seven hours on 26 percent more nights, and their grade point average went up by about 0.08 points.

mainIdea.s: College students who earned small nightly rewards got more rest over four weeks. Their grades jumped sharply, and those gains lasted for years after the payments ended.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the grades rose only modestly, by about 0.08 points. The effect on grades wore off after the next semester.

mainIdea.s: A university moved its morning classes to later in the day so that tired students could rest. Sleep scientists then tracked attendance and test scores over a full year.
mainIdea.why: No classes were moved. Students were paid for each night they slept at least seven hours, and trackers measured their sleep.

tf.s: Researchers handed out sleep trackers to more than 1,100 students.
tf.why: The trackers recorded how long each student slept, and 468 of the students could earn money for good nights.

tf.s: The paid students earned about $50 for each good night of sleep.
tf.why: They earned about $5 for each night of at least seven hours, and they kept up part of the habit after the money stopped.

tf.s: Before the study, half of the students usually stayed up past 1 a.m.
tf.why: The students slept 6.6 hours a night on average and fell short of seven hours on most school nights.

tf.s: The paid students' grade point average went up by about two points.
tf.why: It went up by only about 0.08 points that semester, which is a modest gain.

tf.s: The study came out in the Journal of Political Economy in July.
tf.why: It came out in July 2026 and drew wide attention in September.

tf.s: The effect on grades lasted for many years after the payments ended.
tf.why: Grades stayed higher the next semester, but the effect wore off after that.

lines.text: Did you see that sleep study that {{came out}} in July?
The one where students got paid to sleep? [[Easy money]].
It's not that simple. They got about five dollars for each night of at least seven hours.
Five dollars? That's [[pocket change]]. Did it actually work?
It did. The paid students slept about 19 more minutes on school nights.
Maybe not, but before the study, half of them {{stayed up}} past 1 a.m.
Maybe some of them. The paid students also {{cut back on}} screens late at night.
So did the extra sleep {{pay off}} at school?
A little. Their grade point average {{went up}} by about 0.08 points.
That's small, but for a few dollars a night, it sounds like [[money well spent]].
First-year students {{stood out}}. They had the biggest gains.
They're new to living on their own. What happened when the money stopped?
Many {{kept up}} part of the habit, about eight extra minutes a night. But the boost to grades {{wore off}} after the next semester.
Did the bedtime reminders help on their own?
Not much. Almost everyone wanted more sleep. The hard part was {{following through}}.
Well, I'm going to [[hit the hay]] early tonight. No money needed.
